checkpoints: A fixed sleep inside one worker process only paces that single process's own request pace.
Once the crawler is sharded across many fetchers, five workers each sleeping a second on their own still hit one host five times a second combined, causing the host to rate-limit the whole IP range.
The fix is to move the politeness clock into shared state: keep host:lastFetched in Redis so every worker reads and computes against the same number.
Every worker computes wait = delay - (now - lastFetched), clamped with max(0, …) so a request proceeds for free once enough time has already elapsed.
This formula measures the actual gap between any two requests to the host, not a fixed tick repeated independently inside each worker, making it the only correct approach under any worker count.
The cost is one Redis round-trip per fetch, but the SET is atomic and survives restarts, so it is well worth paying.
An exact in-memory hash set of seen URLs works fine at thousands of URLs but costs 20+ GB of RAM at hundreds of millions of URLs.
The exact set is per-worker, so every fetcher re-discovers duplicates that another fetcher already saw, since the set isn't shared.
A bloom filter stores membership in about 12 bits per item — roughly 120 MB at a 1% error rate for 100 million URLs — a memory win of more than 20x, driven by m bits and k hash functions.
Unlike the exact set, the bloom filter runs as one shared service across all workers, so fetchers stop re-discovering duplicates another worker already saw.

The key property is asymmetry: a bloom filter can return a false positive but never a false negative — BF.ADD only flips bits to 1 and they never flip back, so if the bloom filter says 'not seen,' the URL provably was never added.
A crawler can tolerate skipping a rare URL via a false positive (about 1 in 100) but must never re-fetch a URL it already crawled, and the false positive is the bloom filter's only error mode.

Outlinks are the current state of a page, not an accumulating history — the set returned by `extractOutlinks()` on each parse represents exactly what the page links to right now, and any write path that only inserts treats the link table as an append-only log instead of a snapshot.

`this.linkRepo.save(records)` in `parse()` never deletes prior rows for the same `fromUrl`, so re-crawling a page only ever adds edges: parsing `a` when it links to `b` and `c` writes `a→b` and `a→c`, and if `a` is re-parsed later linking only to `c`, the stale `a→b` row is left sitting in `page_link` alongside the newly written `a→c` row.

Because PageRank computes `PR(u)` by summing contributions over `in(u)`, every stale inbound edge left behind by a shrinking outlink set inflates the in-degree — and therefore the PageRank — of the target URL, even though that URL is no longer actually linked to.

This bug produces no exception or error of any kind, so it drifts silently over months of re-crawls; the only observable symptom is that rankings on a real corpus gradually stop making sense, which makes it very hard to trace back to its source.

The correct replacement semantic is delete-then-insert: before saving the newly extracted records, delete every existing row where the source column equals the page being re-parsed (e.g. `this.linkRepo.delete({ fromUrl: url })`), then insert the fresh outlink set, so the table always converges to exactly the current outlinks rather than a superset of every set ever seen.

An upsert keyed on `(fromUrl, toUrl)` is not a substitute for the delete step — it correctly updates or inserts rows whose pair already appears in the new set, but it does nothing to a row whose pair is simply absent from the new set, since that pair was never part of the new batch being upserted at all.

A delete-then-insert write path is idempotent under re-parsing: running `parse()` any number of times against the same HTML always leaves `page_link` holding exactly the current outlink set for that page, never accumulating duplicates or leftovers from earlier parses.

The fix can be verified concretely by re-parsing the same page with a smaller outlink set than a previous parse and asserting that both `storedLinks` and the actual row count in `page_link` for that `fromUrl` equal the new, smaller count — not the cumulative total of every parse ever run on that page.
Storing the full HTML as a plain text column inline in the same row as url/host/statusCode means each row's size is dominated by the page body rather than the small metadata fields.
Once a text value exceeds roughly 2 KB, Postgres moves it out-of-line into TOAST storage, which bloats the table's physical footprint and skews the query planner's row-width statistics.

Because TOAST bloat and skewed statistics affect the whole table, metadata-only queries such as listing pages or looking up by host slow down even though they never select htmlBody, since they still scan a table whose rows are secretly huge.

Separating the heavy blob from the hot metadata fixes the root cause: push the raw HTML to object storage such as S3 or MinIO under a key derived from the page (e.g. a hash of the URL or a UUID), and keep only a content digest plus that object key in the page row alongside url/host/statusCode/contentType.
A content digest — a hash of the HTML body — doubles as a cheap way to detect duplicate or unchanged pages without re-reading the full HTML on every crawl.

With the blob moved out, the write path still upserts a small metadata row as before, but the body write goes through an object-storage put call instead of populating htmlBody, so a metadata scan now touches a table of small, fixed-width-ish rows with no TOAST involvement.

Inline text storage is not inherently wrong and is genuinely fine at demo or small scale; the trade-off only tips toward object storage at billions of rows, where the extra network hop to fetch the body when actually needed (rendering, re-parsing, re-indexing) and the added consistency burden between Postgres and the object store are worth paying to keep the frequently-queried metadata table small and fast.

The migration's benefit can be verified concretely by comparing metadata-query latency and table-plus-TOAST size before and after the change, and by confirming the HTML is still retrievable end-to-end through its stored object key.

The `enqueue` method issues `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` as three separate awaited Redis calls with no atomicity between them, so two workers enqueuing the same brand-new URL can both read the membership check as a miss before either has run `BF.ADD`, and both then push the URL onto the ZSET as a duplicate.

Each enqueue on this path pays three sequential network round trips to Redis (one for the existence check, one for the bloom add, one for the queue add), and because each awaited call must finish before the next starts, that round-trip count directly caps how many URLs the frontier can accept per second.

The check-and-set can be made atomic and single-round-trip by fusing `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` into one Lua script and registering it as a custom ioredis command (for example via `redis.defineCommand`), since Redis runs a Lua script as one atomic, single-threaded server-side operation.

Because the fused script runs as a single atomic unit, no second worker can observe the bloom filter mid-check, which closes the double-add race entirely, and replacing three awaited calls with one round trip raises enqueue throughput roughly 10x.

Bloom-filter dedup for a crawler is inherently best-effort, so an occasional double-enqueued brand-new URL is generally harmless — the Lua-script fuse is worth making specifically when exactly-once enqueue semantics are required or the system is throughput-bound on enqueue, not as a default change to every code path.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by concurrently calling enqueue with the same brand-new URL from many clients and asserting the queue's size grows by exactly one instead of accumulating duplicate entries.

The throughput claim can be verified by benchmarking enqueues-per-second on the original three-call sequential path versus the single fused Lua-script call, comparing the numbers before and after the change.
The design cleanly separates two orthogonal signals — relevance and authority — from a combiner function.
Relevance is scored at query time with TF-IDF or BM25 over the query's candidate set, and does not exist until a query arrives.
Authority (PageRank) is precomputed in batch and served from a table as an O(1) lookup — the same batch-compute-serve split as the page_rank table's GET /rank/:url.

The contract is a final scorer: final_score = f(relevance, authority), where f starts as a weighted sum and can later become a learned-to-rank model, so pages both relevant and authoritative outrank those with only one property.

Authority can't be computed online because it needs the whole link graph and a full power-iteration pass, whereas relevance only ever scans the retrieved candidate set and never the whole corpus — this cost asymmetry is exactly why one signal is precomputed batch and the other is query-time.

The interface is extensible: it takes a document plus its precomputed features and a query, so adding a new signal like vector-similarity or click-through later is just another input to f — the contract's shape doesn't change, only the number of terms f combines.

A standard bloom filter is append-only — bits only ever flip from 0 to 1, never back — so a URL once marked seen can never become eligible for re-crawl again; that's fine for one-shot dedup but wrong for a crawler that must revisit pages that changed and recognize new items in a feed it already indexed.
The seen-set interface keeps the same two operations the frontier already uses: seen(url) and markSeen(url).
Under the hood it is not one bloom filter but N time-bucketed blooms, for example one per day.
A seen(url) check unions (ORs) the result across all N buckets.
markSeen(url) writes only into the current bucket.
On a schedule, the oldest bucket is dropped and a fresh one opened, so a URL ages out after N buckets and becomes eligible for re-crawl again — giving dedup a TTL without needing a per-url delete.

If an explicit, on-demand un-seen is needed instead (e.g., an RSS poller identifying exactly which item changed), the alternative is a Cuckoo filter, which supports delete at the cost of slightly higher memory per item than a bloom filter.

The sizing discipline mirrors the frontier's single bloom: size each bucket's capacity to the expected unique URLs in that window times roughly 1.5, and rotate at around 80% occupancy, so the real false-positive rate never drifts far above the advertised one.
Sorting by viewCount measures traffic, not authority.
A spam farm with auto-clicks can climb to the top of a viewCount-based ranking even though no one actually trusts it, showing why viewCount fails as an authority signal.
Authority is a distinct, recursive property: a page is authoritative when other authoritative pages link to it (Larry Page's 1998 insight).

PageRank turns that recursion into a computable recurrence over the directed link graph: each page distributes its current rank across its outlinks, so a page that many trusted pages point to accumulates a high score.
Keeping the graph honest requires extracting absolute outlinks from each page.
Repeated links within the same page must be deduped so they count as one edge, not ten.
Self-links must be dropped, since a self-link would grant a page a free rank boost.
The resulting ranking reflects trustworthiness — exactly what the product question is really asking for — not raw view count.
A 5xx on /robots.txt means you cannot read the host's policy, so RFC 9309 says treat it as deny-all, since refusing to crawl is safer than over-crawling on a transient failure.
You must not cache that 5xx response as "allow everything," or a momentary blip opens the floodgates.
A Crawl-delay of 300 seconds should never block a worker thread for five minutes, since that pins a scarce fetcher doing nothing.
Instead, push the URL back to the frontier with a notBefore timestamp and let the worker pull other ready work, so a scheduler picks it up once its time arrives.
Both edge cases share the same theme: politeness decisions must never waste a fetcher or over-trust a failure.
Key the robots cache by the full hostname, since sub-domains publish independent robots files.
Running the bloom check before the ZADD means the queue only ever holds URLs the crawler has not yet seen.
That keeps the expensive structure — the ZSET, which stores full URL strings — small, while the cheap structure — the bloom, about 12 bits per URL — absorbs the deduplication.

Reversing the order (enqueue first, dedupe on dequeue) leaves a duplicate URL sitting in the ZSET from the moment it's enqueued until it's popped and rejected, inflating queueSize with dead weight and defeating the entire point of using a bloom filter to save memory.
The ZSET answers "what should I crawl next?" (priority ordering), while the bloom answers "have I already seen this?" — two different questions.
The atomic highest-score pop via ZPOPMAX hands N workers distinct URLs with no race.
Separating ordering from dedup is what lets the frontier scale past 100M URLs on commodity memory.
Recording each duplicate to an indexed audit trail turns the dedup rate into a queryable metric.
A sudden spike in that metric flags a redirect loop, a broken parser, or an overflowed bloom filter — none of which is observable if you only ever look at the queue.
